This prepares them to read about ancient Greece in Lesson 2 and to meet Percy Jackson's world in *The Lightning Thief*.","enduringUnderstanding":"Stories carry a culture's questions, fears, hopes, and values, and readers can infer those values from the clues in the words.","futureLessons":"Students return to their working definition of *myth* as they read about ancient Greece (Lesson 2) and compare ancient myths with Riordan's modern retelling in the anchor text.","performanceTask":"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, students analyze what myths and modern adaptations show about cultural values. Today's inference work with unlabeled passages builds curiosity and starts the idea that myths explain the world."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"myth","definition":"a traditional story, often about gods, heroes, or nature, that explains something about the world or a culture's beliefs","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"mythology","definition":"a collection of myths from a culture, or the study of myths (from *mythos*, story + *logy*, study of)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"infer","definition":"to figure out something by combining clues in the text with what you already know","tier":"support"},{"word":"values","definition":"beliefs about what is important, right, or good","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"What Are Myths?","author":"Newsela Staff","pages":"Full article"},{"title":"Prometheus/Pandora myth passages (three short, unlabeled excerpts)","author":"Olive Coolidge","pages":"Three short excerpts, teacher-provided"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students read \"What Are Myths?\" and share initial ideas about why cultures create stories about gods, nature, danger, or the unknown, recording a first definition of *myth*.","activities":[{"id":"launch-read-what-are-myths","title":"Read and Record: What Is a Myth?","minutes":8,"standards":["RI.6.1","SL.6.1.a"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"What Are Myths?","pages":"Full article"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read \"What Are Myths?\" Underline one sentence that explains why people told myths. Then, in your Journal, write your first definition of *myth* in your own words. Leave space below it; you will add to it later."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"We are starting a unit about a boy who discovers that Greek gods are real. Before we meet him, let's find out where those stories came from."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this fast. Students read silently or in pairs for about 4 minutes. Walk the room and note the sentences students underline. A first definition can be rough; they will revise it at the end of the Lesson."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"According to the article, why might people create stories about gods, nature, danger, or the unknown?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The article says people told myths to explain things they couldn't understand, like storms or why the seasons change. If you didn't know the science, a story about a god made sense."}]},{"id":"launch-whole-class-ideas","title":"Whole-Class Initial Ideas","minutes":7,"standards":["SL.6.1.a","SL.6.1"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Use Think-Pair-Share. Share your underlined sentence and your first definition of *myth* with a partner. Then listen as the class builds a list of reasons cultures create myths."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What do you think people felt when they faced something dangerous or unknown, like a flood or a long winter? How might a story help?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They probably felt scared. A story could make it feel less random, like there was a reason, or someone in charge you could pray to."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Hold onto that idea. Fear, hope, and the need to explain things will help you read the next texts like a detective."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Chart student reasons on the board under the heading \"Why Cultures Create Stories.\" Expect: explain nature, teach lessons, comfort people, explain danger. Do not reveal the word *mythology* or the source of the passages yet."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Students infer meaning from three unlabeled Prometheus/Pandora passages, share theories, then revise their definition of *myth* after the teacher reveals the morphology of *mythology* and the source myths.","activities":[{"id":"lia-mystery-passages","title":"Part A: Mystery Passages","minutes":15,"standards":["RI.6.1","RI.6.4","SL.6.1.a"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"Three unlabeled passages from Coolidge's Prometheus/Pandora myths","pages":"Teacher-provided handout"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"You are going to read three short passages with no titles and no background. Treat them as mystery clues. Your job is to infer, which means using clues in the words to figure out what the story is really about."},{"type":"directions","text":"In groups of three or four, read each passage and annotate it. Circle words or phrases that seem important. Underline evidence that answers each question. Write the question number in the margin next to your evidence. Question 1: What problem is this passage trying to explain? Question 2: What kind of world does this story imagine? Question 3: What clues hint at fear, hope, or cultural values?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"When a word is unfamiliar, use the words around it. If a passage says a god *chained* someone to a rock as punishment, you can tell *chained* means held in place so they cannot leave, even if you have never seen the word before."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What problem might this passage be trying to explain?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Maybe why people have fire, or why there is suffering in the world. The passage says people lived without fire, then someone brought it, and the gods got angry."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What kind of world does this story imagine?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A world where gods are powerful and watch humans. They can punish anyone who breaks their rules, and what they do causes things to happen in nature."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which words or phrases hint at fear, hope, or values?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The word *punished* hints at fear of the gods. The part where hope stays in the jar hints that people valued hope even when things were bad."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RI.6.1"],"stem":"A group reads a passage where a box is opened and troubles fly out, but one small thing stays inside. Which annotation best uses text evidence to support the inference that the story values hope?","choices":[{"text":"The group circles the box because boxes are usually used to store things.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is a general fact about boxes, not evidence from the passage about what the story values."},{"text":"The group underlines the detail that hope stays inside after the troubles escape and writes that hope is treated as something precious.","correct":true,"rationale":"This connects a specific detail to an inference about values, which is what citing evidence for an inference requires."},{"text":"The group writes that the passage is about a curious person.","correct":false,"rationale":"Curiosity may be in the passage, but this note does not cite evidence or address values."},{"text":"The group underlines the first sentence because the first sentence is always the most important.","correct":false,"rationale":"Importance depends on meaning, not position; this gives no reasoning about the question."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students use evidence-based language and expanded noun phrases to explain what unlabeled passages suggest about the world of the story.","sayAsk":"Model: \"The word *punished* suggests the gods are powerful and frightening.\" Offer frames: \"The phrase ___ suggests ___ because ___.\" \"This story imagines a world where ___.\" \"The ___ gods / ___ gift shows ___.\" Encourage students to expand noun phrases: \"gods\" becomes \"powerful, angry gods who punish people.\" Allow students to discuss first in their home language, then say the idea in English.","watchFor":"If students only copy a quote, then prompt: \"What does that make you think? Start with 'This suggests...'\" If students use bare nouns (fire, gods), then prompt: \"Add a describing word or phrase.\" Success: students pair a quoted phrase with an inference and use at least one expanded noun phrase."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Starting the inference","tryThis":"Give a two-column organizer: \"Clue from the passage\" and \"What it makes me think.\" Complete the first row together, then let the group continue."},{"situation":"Struggling with: Unfamiliar older vocabulary","tryThis":"Model circling the word, reading the sentence before and after, and guessing a synonym. Provide a short glossary only after students have tried to infer."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Analyzing word choice","tryThis":"Ask: Which word in the passage has the strongest connotation, positive or negative, and how does it shape how readers feel about the gods or humans?"}]}]},{"id":"lia-share-theories","title":"Part B: Share Theories and Reveal the Sources","minutes":15,"standards":["L.6.4.b","RI.6.4","SL.6.1","SL.6.1.a"],"routine":"Huddle","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Join a class huddle. Each group shares one theory about what the passages are and why they were told. Cite your annotated evidence. When another group speaks, add on with \"I agree because...\" or \"I would add...\""},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is your group's theory about what these three passages are, and what clue convinced you?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"We think they are old stories explaining where fire and trouble came from. The clue is that gods act like people, with anger and punishments, but they control nature."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Great detective work. These passages come from Coolidge's retellings of the Prometheus and Pandora myths, which are Greek stories told more than two thousand years ago. Notice how your theory matches what the article said about why myths are created."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Let's look at the word *mythology*. It comes from two Greek parts: *mythos*, which means story, and *logy*, which means study of. Think of *biology*: *bio* means life and *logy* means study of, so biology is the study of life. So *mythology* means the study of myths, or a culture's collection of myths."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Using the same pattern, what do you think *geology* or *zoology* means if *geo* means earth and *zoo* means animal?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Geology is the study of the earth, like rocks and mountains, and zoology is the study of animals."},{"type":"directions","text":"Return to your first definition of *myth* from the Launch. Add to it using what you learned from the passages and the word *mythology*. Include at least one reason cultures created myths and one example from the passages."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A myth is a traditional story that explains something people could not understand, like where fire came from. Myths show what a culture feared, hoped for, and valued. For example, the passage where hope stays in the jar shows people valued hope."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Do not worry if student theories differ from the sources. Credit reasoning backed by evidence."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in building on others' ideas and in connecting word parts to meaning when evaluating how words express ideas.","sayAsk":"Offer frames: \"I agree with ___ because the passage says ___.\" \"Another clue is ___.\" \"The root *logy* means ___, so *mythology* means ___.\" Have students say the roots aloud chorally. For noun phrases, model: \"stories\" becomes \"ancient stories about powerful gods.\"","watchFor":"If students restate a group's idea without evidence, then prompt: \"Which words in the passage show that?\" If students confuse *myth* and *mythology*, then prompt: \"Which one is a single story? Which is the whole collection or study?\" Success: students use the root to explain *mythology* and cite evidence when building on a peer's idea."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Roots and affixes","tryThis":"Show *bio + logy* and *myth + ology* side by side on the board with arrows to meanings. Ask students to find one more *logy* word."},{"situation":"Struggling with: Building on a peer's idea","tryThis":"Provide the frames \"I agree because...\" and \"I would add...\" on a card, and have the student read the peer's evidence aloud before responding."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Using roots","tryThis":"Ask: What other words do you know that end in *logy* or *ology*? Use the root to predict what each means, then check a dictionary."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students revisit their definition of myth and reflect on how evidence supported their thinking.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-quick-write","title":"Quick Write: What Is a Myth?","minutes":5,"standards":["RI.6.1","L.6.4.b"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Write for four minutes: How would you now explain to a friend what a myth is and what *mythology* means? Include one clue from the passages that helped you infer what the story was about."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What clue in the passages most changed your thinking about what myths are for?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The part about hope staying in the jar changed my thinking. I thought myths were only about explaining nature, but they also show what people believed in and valued. Mythology is the study of these stories."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework","purpose":"Optional extension: students apply the idea that stories explain the unknown.","activities":[{"id":"homework-explain-world","title":"Optional: Explain Something with a Story","minutes":0,"standards":["RI.6.1"],"blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Optional: Think of something in nature you wonder about, such as thunder or the moon. In your Journal, write three sentences of a short myth-style explanation. Then write one sentence saying what fear, hope, or value your story shows. Alternatively, read your independent reading book for 20 minutes."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students read \"What Are Myths?\" to build initial ideas about why cultures create stories, then infer meaning from three unlabeled Prometheus/Pandora passages by annotating evidence. After sharing theories, they learn the morphology of *mythology* (*mythos* + *logy*, like *biology*) and revise their definition of *myth*.","keyActivities":["Read \"What Are Myths?\" and record a first definition","Annotate three unlabeled Prometheus/Pandora passages to infer problem, world, and cultural values","Huddle to share theories and reveal source myths","Mini Morphology Move: mythology as study of myths","Revise definition of myth in a Quick Write"],"vocabularyTaught":["myth","mythology","infer","values"],"standardsCovered":["L.6.4.b","RI.6.1","RI.6.4","SL.6.1.a","SL.6.1"]}}
